corrected_claim.text: The seed row says the positions of Kilpatrick and Merritt on Jul 1 were not found. The Official Records give them (no hour): Kilpatrick's division marched on Jul 1 from Hanover by Abbottstown to Berlin to intercept Stuart and failed (a detachment under Lt. Col. A. J. Alexander pursued Stuart to Rossville; the 1st West Virginia Cavalry went 10 miles beyond Berlin and moved back the same night); Merritt's Reserve Brigade was at Mechanicstown picketing the mountain roads until it marched to Emmitsburg on Jul 2; the Cavalry Corps headquarters was at Taneytown (dispatches of Jul 1 are dated there); Gregg's Second Division marched from Manchester to Hanover Junction, McIntosh's and J. I. Gregg's brigades going on to Hanover and Huey's returning to Manchester. NOT documented: any hour of these marches, where Pleasonton himself was, the road of Merritt's pickets. One list in Custer's report puts the engagement at Hunterstown on Jul 1 (Battery M), against Jul 2 at sundown in Kilpatrick's own summary: carried as two scenarios.
corrected_claim.marking: positions by day: documented; hours: gap; Hunterstown date: two scenarios, no default

sub_claims.claim: Kilpatrick's division marched on Jul 1 to Berlin by Abbottstown to intercept Stuart, but failed
A detachment under Lt. Col. A. J. Alexander (chief of staff) pursued Stuart to Rossville (Pleasonton spells it Rosstown)
The 1st West Virginia Cavalry of Kilpatrick's First Brigade marched to Abbottstown, then to Berlin and a point 10 miles beyond, and moved back on the night of the same day without finding the enemy

Merritt's Reserve Brigade lay near Mechanicstown, Md. (picketing, scouting and patrolling the mountain roads) and marched from Mechanicstown to Emmitsburg on Jul 2, so it was there at the end of Jul 1
The Cavalry Corps headquarters was at Taneytown on Jul 1 (orders to Buford, Kilpatrick, Gregg and Merritt dated there; no hour printed)

Gregg's Second Division: headquarters at Hanover Junction on Jul 1; at 11.55 a.m. the Corps ordered the forces drawn in from Hanover Junction to Manchester; McIntosh's and J. I. Gregg's brigades went on to Hanover, Huey's returned to Manchester
Pleasonton's own position on Jul 1 (the person, as against the headquarters at Taneytown)
The hour of Kilpatrick's march, of Alexander's pursuit and of Merritt's position

corrected_claim.text: Wainwright joined Doubleday at about 10.30 a. m. and moved the three batteries with him across the fields toward the seminary. The Third Division reached the field toward 11 (Rowley): Biddle's brigade about 11 a. m., formed on the extreme left a third of a mile in front of the seminary facing west (the 151st Pennsylvania, 10.30 a. m.); Stone posted his brigade at 11 a. m. between the two brigades of Wadsworth's division, right on the Chambersburg road and left nearly to the wood held by Meredith; the 150th Pennsylvania gives about noon. Robinson's division was placed in reserve near the seminary and the First Brigade (Paul) set to intrench the ridge; Baxter reached the front at 11 a. m. Doubleday directed Robinson to the seminary, sent Stone to the open space on the right of the wood and Biddle to the left and rear of the Iron Brigade toward the Millerstown road, Rowley having charge of that part of the line. CORRECTED: Rowley did not take command of the division on Jul 1: his report says the command had devolved on him the day previous (Jun 30). NOT documented: the hour at which each battery of the Artillery Brigade came up.
corrected_claim.marking: arrival hours by regiment: documented; the Jul 1 change of division command: contradicted (Jun 30)

sub_claims.claim: Wainwright's Artillery Brigade: about 10.30 a. m. Wainwright joined Doubleday and by his order moved the three batteries remaining with him across the fields toward the seminary; the Third Division with Cooper's battery arrived soon afterward

Third Division, First (Biddle's) Brigade: about 11 a. m. within a mile of the town, then formed on the extreme left, a third of a mile in front of the seminary and facing west; the 151st Pennsylvania of that brigade formed at 10.30 a. m.; the version of Biddle's report dated Jul 2 and printed in Pennsylvania at Gettysburg has the brigade reaching the front about 11 a. m.

Third Division, Second (Stone's) Brigade: posted at 11 a. m. between the two brigades of Wadsworth's division, right on the Chambersburg road and left nearly to the wood held by Meredith (Dana: into position about 11 a. m.)
Rowley: toward 11 o'clock the two portions of the Third Division reached the field from the south and took positions on the right and left of the seminary, half a mile or more west of it

Doubleday's dispositions: Robinson in reserve at the seminary with slight intrenchments; Stone to the open space on the right of the wood between Cutler and Meredith; Biddle on the left and rear of the Iron Brigade toward the Millerstown road; Rowley in charge of that part of the line

Second Division (Robinson): placed in reserve near the seminary; Baxter's brigade reached the front at 11 a. m.; the First (Paul's) Brigade, massed near the railroad embankment at about 11 a. m., was set to intrench the ridge of the seminary

corrected_claim.text: On reaching the field Carter's and Fry's batteries were ordered to a high point in front of Rodes' lines to enfilade the Union lines and batteries; Carter's own battery, exposed, had 4 men killed outright and 7 severely wounded (OCR "'7"); Page's battery, ordered to the left, opened on the infantry advancing on O'Neal, came under the oblique fire of Union artillery in the valley north of the town, and lost 2 killed, 2 mortally wounded, 26 badly wounded and 17 horses. Rodes says Carter's battalion "soon opened fire" as the division moved by the right flank; Ewell that it opened with fine effect on the flank of the Union force engaged with Hill. NOT documented in the Official Records: the hour (12:30 in the seed); the name Oak Hill is the National Park Service's (Rodes: "a prominent hill on the ridge"); any loss figure of Fry's battery (Carter gives none). The hour is secondary only (by noon / 1 o'clock).
corrected_claim.marking: event and losses: documented (Carter); hour: inferred, secondary sources only; name Oak Hill: National Park Service

time_window.text: Jul 1, morning: the division left Cashtown at 5 a. m. and was nearing Gettysburg at about 9 (no hour of the brigades' arrival); the brigades advance at 2 p. m.
time_window.basis: Heth OR27-2-R549 p.637 and p.638; Hill R534 p.607; Jones (Pettigrew's brigade) R550 pp.642-643. Window limits: the start 09:00 is the hour at which Heth, already near Gettysburg, says he was still ignorant of the force there (about 9 o'clock; Heth R549 p.637); the brigades marched behind Archer's and Davis's; the end 14:00 is the hour at which Pettigrew's brigade was ordered to advance after standing in line of battle in the woods (2 p. m., Jones R550 p.643); the arrival is before it. A limit is an allowed bound, not a claim of when the event happened; the reader adds its own clock tolerance at a clock-time limit.

corrected_claim.text: Heth's division, with Pegram's battalion, was ordered to move from Cashtown at 5 a. m. on Jul 1; Heth, nearing the town, was at about 9 o'clock still ignorant of the force there. When Archer's and Davis's brigades were put in line within a mile of Gettysburg, Pettigrew's brigade and Heth's old brigade under Colonel Brockenbrough were held in reserve. Pettigrew's brigade moved down the pike early on the morning of Jul 1, deployed about 2.5 miles from the town, crossed to the right of the pike (other regiments having been engaged for some time), took position behind the batteries for about half an hour, advanced half a mile to a skirt of woods and stood in line of battle until orders to advance came at 2 p. m., with Brockenbrough's brigade on its left. The seed's "arrive at Herr Ridge about 12:30" has no support in any report read: the brigades were with the division from the morning. NOT documented: the minute of their arrival or an arrival at Herr Ridge by that name (the 12:30 hour rests on Wikipedia only).

corrected_claim.text: Howard received orders at 3.30 a. m. to bring the Eleventh Corps within supporting distance and at 8 a. m. the order to march to Gettysburg; Schurz's Third Division left camp at 7 a. m. by Horner's Mills. Dilger's battery arrived at about 10 a. m. (Osborn: a little after 10), Bancroft's battery at 11 a. m., the 45th New York at 11 a. m., Schurz himself about 11.30. Howard places the head of the corps "about this time" after 12.30 p. m.; the First Division came by the Emmitsburg road proper (the 75th Ohio about 1 p. m., the 17th Connecticut between 1 and 2); Steinwehr reached the field at about 2 o'clock; Schurz had the first two divisions deployed about 2 p. m. NOT documented: Howard's expectation of the corps "a little after one"; the Baltimore pike as a route (the Third Division's own report prints a blank for its hour of arrival). The hour of the "head" is carried as scenarios.

Willis) was at once placed in line of battle "say at 12 o'clock" (the OCR text prints 13; the page image reads 12) as the enemy made a demonstration in its front, so the formation is carried as two scenarios, about noon (4th Georgia) and about 1 p. m. corrected_claim.event: Lee comes to the field in the afternoon: Pendleton's hour (as Early reports it) is about 2 p. m., Longstreet's about 3, and Fremantle joined him and Hill on the ridge at 4.30; Heth obtained Lee's permission to attack while Rodes was engaged (Early's report of Heth); Lee's instruction to avoid a general engagement is documented

time_window.text: Jul 1 afternoon: about 14:00 to 16:30 (13:30 is the delegated default, marked a gap)
time_window.basis: Lee OR27-2-R426 pp.317-318; Ewell R467 p.444; Early in SHSP vol.6 (Heth and Pendleton as reported); Longstreet 1896; Fremantle 1864; SHSP vol.4 (letter of Apr 5, 1876). Window limits: the start 13:30 is the PDF value 13:30, which is the delegated default (C-042) and is kept as the first view, marked a gap: no text read gives an hour before 14:00; the end 16:30 is the hour at which Fremantle, arriving with Longstreet, joined Lee and Hill on the ridge (4.30 p. m., diary of Jul 1); Lee was on the field by then. A limit is an allowed bound, not a claim of when the event happened; the reader adds its own clock tolerance at a clock-time limit.

corrected_claim.text: No report of the Official Records gives the hour of Lee's arrival. Participants give: about two P. M. (Pendleton, as Early reports it in the Southern Historical Society Papers), from about three o'clock (Longstreet, 1896), on the ridge with Hill by 4.30 p. m. (Fremantle, diary of Jul 1), near the close of the battle soon after Anderson's division arrived (an unsigned letter of 1876). Documented: Lee had told Ewell he did not want a general engagement brought on till the rest of the army came up (Ewell) and his report says a general battle so far from the base had not been intended unless attacked; Hill ordered Heth's advance (Lee). Heth "applied for and obtained permission from General Lee to attack while Rodes was engaged" (Early quoting Heth, 1878). NOT supported: that Lee found at his arrival the restriction ignored; that Heth's request was first refused; any arrival at "Herr Ridge" by that name; the hour 13:30 or 14:30 (seed values; Wikipedia and a secondary site).
corrected_claim.marking: Lee's presence on the field in the afternoon: documented (Fremantle by 4.30); arrival hour: inferred (participants disagree), delegated default 13:30 marked a gap

sub_claims.claim: Lee was on the ridge with Hill when Fremantle, arriving with Longstreet, came in sight of Gettysburg at 4.30 p. m.
Pendleton: Lee arrived on the field about two P. M. and gave instructions for posting artillery (as Early reports it, 1878)
Longstreet (1896): Lee was on the field from about three o'clock of the afternoon of the first day

An unsigned letter of Apr 5, 1876 printed in the Southern Historical Society Papers: Lee and staff arrived near the close of the battle on the afternoon of Jul 1, soon after Anderson's division; Meade's Life and Letters (1913): Lee reached Seminary Ridge about half-past four
Heth applied for and obtained permission from Lee to attack while Rodes was engaged (Early's report of Heth's statement)

Lee had told Ewell that he did not want a general engagement brought on till the rest of the army came up; his report: a general battle so far from the base had not been intended unless attacked; Ewell was told to avoid a general engagement until the other divisions came up
Hill, not Lee, ordered Heth to advance (Lee's report)
Lee learns on arrival that the restriction on bringing on a general engagement had been ignored; Heth's request refused and then allowed
Arrival at Herr Ridge at 13:30 (PDF, secondary "SS") or at 14:30 (Wikipedia)

corrected_claim.text: Early, on arriving in sight of Gettysburg on the Heidlersburg road, found Rodes' division engaged with the enemy to the right of him and "immediately ordered my troops to the front" and formed his line across the Heidlersburg road, with Gordon on the right, Hoke's brigade (under Colonel Avery) on the left, Hays in the centre, Smith's in rear of Hoke's; Jones' battalion of artillery was posted on the left of the road in front of Hoke and opened on the enemy's infantry and artillery. Hays (arrived within a mile and a half of the town) says that when his line was formed Gordon "a little after 2 o'clock, was ordered to advance"; Gordon puts the order to move forward in support of Rodes' left at about 3 p. m. The force first met was "a diviision of the Eleventh Corps, commanded by Brigadier-General Barlow" (Early; "the hill on which Barlow had been posted"). NOT documented: any hour of the deployment itself (13:30 in the seed is a National Park Service value); "opposite XI Corps" at the moment of forming is Early's identification after the fight.

corrected_claim.text: No report of Rodes' division gives one hour for its attack. Confederate regimental reports date the engagement from about noon (26th Alabama: engaged the enemy about 12 m.; 2nd North Carolina Battalion between 12 m. and 1 p. m.; the 53rd North Carolina in line about 1 o'clock). Doubleday (Union clock) has Ewell's forces advancing about 1.30 p. m. in two deployed lines supported by a third; Lee, Hill and Howard date the arrival of Rodes' or Ewell's force on the field at 2.30 (Howard 2.45 for the enemy in force in front of the Eleventh Corps); Davis about 3; the Battles and Leaders article has Rodes give the order to attack at 2.30 p. m. and a Pennsylvania regiment dates Iverson's advance about 2.30; the National Park Service CLR has the four brigades advance beginning around 2:30. The row's "uncoordinated" attack is Rodes' and Ewell's own account of the Alabama brigade (confusion, direction different from orders). All hours are carried as scenarios; the delegated default is 14:00 inside the window 13:30-14:30 and is not changed here.

Lee: about 2.30 p. m. the advance of Ewell's corps, Rodes' division with Carter's battalion, arrived by the Middletown road and formed on Heth's left; Hill: about 2.30 the right wing of Ewell's corps appeared on his left; Howard: about 2.45 the enemy showed himself in force in front of the Eleventh Corps; Davis: about 3 p. m. a division of Ewell's corps came up on his left

corrected_claim.text: Steinwehr: at about 2 o'clock he arrived with his division near Gettysburg and was ordered to occupy Cemetery Hill, where he found the reserve artillery of the corps in position; he placed Coster's brigade on the north-east end of the hill in support of Wiedrich's battery, which was then in position, and Smith's brigade toward the north-west. The earthwork: Wainwright writes that "at dusk, no attack having been made" the batteries on the hill outside the cemetery gate were posted and "light earthworks thrown up in front of each gun to protect the men from the fire of the enemy's sharpshooters"; Hunt adds that each gun had a small earthwork thrown up in its front for partial shelter. Second pass: Capt. Roath of the 107th Pennsylvania writes that after the engagement the regiment fell back to the left of Cemetery Hill and "threw up strong breastworks, which we occupied until next morning", and Lieut. Whittier (5th Maine Battery) that during the night "temporary earthworks were thrown up covering the pieces" (no hour in either). NOT documented: any digging at 14:00, the dimensions of the works, Wiedrich's own report of intrenchments (none in his report); the seed "begins digging" at 14:00 is contradicted. Per the standing rule no earthwork is placed before this window; the earthwork is shown as built at dusk in front of the guns only.

corrected_claim.text: Rodes: "I caused Iverson's brigade to advance, and at the same moment gave in person to O'Neal the order to attack" and "Iverson's brigade attacked handsomely, but suffered very heavily from the enemy's musketry fire from behind a stone wall along the crest of the ridge". Iverson: his skirmishers were to be hotly engaged before he moved; he received an order to advance to meet the enemy, with Daniel supporting and O'Neal on his left; "Learning that the Alabama brigade, on my left, was moving, I advanced at once, and soon came in contact with the enemy, strongly posted in woods and behind a concealed stone wall", at 100 yards a desperate fight; a gap was on his left; 500 of his men were left dead and wounded in a straight line and nearly all that were left unhurt in three regiments were captured. The Confederate casualty return (OR p.342, read on the page image) prints for Iverson's brigade a total row of 130 killed, 328 wounded, 308 missing and an aggregate of 820; 130 + 328 + 308 is 766, not 820, and the four regiment rows total 455, so the printed columns are inconsistent with one another (130 + 382 + 308 would be 820, so a transposed wounded figure is possible but is not asserted). Iverson and Rodes disagree on who moved first (carried as scenarios, no default). NOT documented: "advances without scouting" (Iverson says he had skirmishers out and waited for them to be hotly engaged), the strength 1,350 (no figure in the reports), Baxter by name at the wall, the hour (14:00-14:30 in the seed).

corrected_claim.text: Iverson and Rodes both say the Union troops fired from behind a stone wall: Iverson found the enemy "strongly posted in woods and behind a concealed stone wall", Rodes that Iverson suffered "from the enemy's musketry fire from behind a stone wall along the crest of the ridge". The 88th Pennsylvania (Baxter's brigade) was drawn up in line of battle along a stone fence; the 97th New York's skirmishers drew fire from a stone wall and the embankment of the road; the 104th New York (Paul's brigade) later drove the enemy from a stone wall covered with thick underbrush and took position behind it. The National Park Service says a stone fence ran along the eastern boundary of the Forney farm on Oak Ridge, that troops used stone fences such as those along Oak Ridge as breastworks and that Baxter's and Paul's brigades lay in part behind overgrown and tumbled-down stone walls there (secondary); Battles and Leaders puts Paul's brigade behind the stone walls of a field facing west and Baxter's facing north. No report says the wall was built during the battle: a pre-existing wall is the inference; no construction animation. The reports do not name Baxter's brigade at "the" wall by that name for the whole line.

corrected_claim.text: The 119th New York started on the road to Gettysburg about 5 a. m. on July 1 and marched "over rough and muddy roads through a drenching rain", reaching Gettysburg about 12 o'clock; the 58th New York, marching with the train, found the roads in a very bad state "as the rain, falling down in torrents" and the rain ceased about 4 miles from Gettysburg before it arrived about 3.30 p. m.; Schurz's Third Division double-quicked into Gettysburg while "the weather was sultry"; Davis says the men were exhausted "by the heat and severity of the engagement"; Colonel Prey (104th New York, in New York at Gettysburg) says that by the time of the move north toward the railroad "the day had become quite showery". corrected_claim.text: Heth: "After resting in line of battle for one hour or more, orders were received to attack the enemy in my front, with the notification that General Pender's division would support me"; the division had not advanced 100 yards before it was hotly engaged; Pettigrew's brigade broke through the enemy's first, second and third lines, and Brockenbrough was held in check on the left for a short time and then drove the enemy in confusion; Archer (Colonel Fry) changed front against cavalry on the right. Jones (Pettigrew's brigade): the brigade stood in line of battle until 2 p. m., "when orders to advance were received", and moved forward with Brockenbrough on its left. Hill: after Ewell's right wing appeared (about 2.30) "Pender's division was then ordered forward". Lee: Heth's troops, having suffered heavily, were relieved by Pender's. The Union side: Rowley holds the position "until nearly 4 o'clock in the afternoon" when "a general advance of the enemy's infantry was now made in two very strong lines"; Doubleday: about 4 p. m. the enemy, strongly re-enforced, advanced in large numbers overlapping the left, pressing the right and overwhelming the centre. NOT documented: Hill's 14:30 as the hour of Heth's attack (Hill's sentence gives it for Ewell's appearance and Pender's order); an attack of Heth and Rodes together on the whole line as one act (the reports describe separate attacks that overlap).

corrected_claim.text: Doubleday directed Robinson to station his division in reserve at the seminary and "to throw up some slight intrenchments", and says the First Brigade of Meredith's and another occupied "the intrenchments in front of the seminary, which I had directed to be thrown up as a precautionary measure"; Robinson set Paul's brigade at work to intrench the ridge; Colonel W. corrected_claim.text: Doubleday sent Robinson with Paul's brigade to Baxter's assistance; part of Paul's brigade was posted as a support to Baxter and part perpendicular to the line; Robinson: "the veteran commander of the First Brigade, Brigadier-General Paul, who fell, severely wounded". That Paul lost both eyes is stated by Bachelder (1873: a bullet passing into one eye and out at the other, totally blind since), by the 16th Maine (shot through both eyes), by Colonel Prey of the 104th New York ("losing the sight of both eyes") and by the 107th/other Pennsylvania address ("losing both eyes"); no report of the Official Records says it. I was ordered to move my brigade forward to the support of Major-General Rodes' left"; the men moved slowly until within about 300 yards of the enemy's line (the OCR prints :>,()(); read as 300 on the page image), then rapidly, over rail and plank fences and a creek, and charged a line on the crest of a hill, part of it woodland. corrected_claim.text: Early: Jones' battalion opened with considerable effect; Gordon was ordered forward in support of Doles, then Hays' and Hoke's brigades in line; "After a short but hot contest, Gordon succeeded in routing the force opposed to him, consisting of a division of the Eleventh Corps, commanded by Brigadier-General Barlow", captured Barlow, "who was severely wounded", and drove the division back with great slaughter; Ewell: Gordon's brigade "after an obstinate contest, broke Barlow's division, captured General Barlow". Schurz: about 3 o'clock the enemy appeared in front with heavy masses of infantry, the Second Brigade, First Division fell back in considerable disorder, Barlow was severely wounded and carried off, the First Brigade, forced back, contested every inch; Ames took the First Division; the orders to withdraw to Cemetery Hill followed. Jones placed twelve guns in position and opened. The First Brigade of Barlow's division is von Gilsa's: the 41st New York (nine companies), 54th and 68th New York and 153rd Pennsylvania. NOT documented: the length of the fight (about 20 minutes or less than an hour: no text read); that Barlow was "shot" (the reports say severely wounded); Ames's "retreat" is his own division's falling back (R244).

Window limits: the start 11:00 is the hour at which Wilkeson's battery came up and went into action (about 11 a. m., Hunt R028 p.230 and Bancroft R269 p.756: Wilkeson fell in the commencement of the contest); the 17th Connecticut came into Gettysburg between 1 and 2 p. m. (Brady R247 p.716), so Fowler's death is after 13:00; the end 15:30 is Schurz's hour for the collapse (after about 3 o'clock) with the retreat to Cemetery Hill after 5 o'clock; no hour of either death is printed. corrected_claim.text: The casualty return lists among the officers killed, Connecticut, "Lieut. Colonel Douglas Fowler, 17th Infantry"; Brady: the regiment (six companies under Lieutenant-Colonel Fowler) advanced with the other regiments of the brigade to the left and front of the town, behind the 107th Ohio, deployed at the double-quick, and "Lieutenant-Colonel Fowler was killed when the regiment advanced and deployed". Wilkeson: Hunt says "About 11 a. m. Wilkeson's battery ... came up, and reported to General Barlow, who posted it close to the enemy's line of infantry ... In the commencement of this unequal contest, Lieut. Bayard Wilkeson ... fell, mortally wounded, and was carried from the field"; Bancroft: the battery reached the town at 11 a. m., engaged on the north side of the York road eastward of the poor-house, and "Lieutenant Wilkeson was struck in the right leg by a shot from the enemy's artillery, and mortally wounded" before the sections retired after half an hour; Howard also records him mortally wounded. The seed's "Col. Douglas Fowler" is Lieutenant-Colonel and "Lt. Col. Baynard Wilkeson" is First Lieutenant Bayard Wilkeson. NOT documented: the hour of either death; that either was in a "counterattack on the knoll".
corrected_claim.marking: names, ranks, deaths: documented; hours: gap; place of Wilkeson: documented (York road); Fowler: north of the town

time_window.text: Jul 1, from about 12:00 into the afternoon; the report gives no hour (the infantry advance through the town came after an hour or more of skirmishing; Gordon's brigade was ordered forward a little after 2 o'clock, Hays)
time_window.basis: Blackford OR27-2-R527 pp.597-598; Rodes R506 p.557; O'Neal R523 p.594; Daniel R507 p.566; Hays R472 p.479; Devin OR27-1-R339 p.939; 45th New York sketch, New York at Gettysburg vol.1 p.378. Window limits: the start 12:00 is the hour at which Rodes' division, marching with the sharpshooters ahead of it, was about 2.5 miles from the town (about 12 m., Daniel R507 p.566); Blackford's corps was deployed 2 miles out; no report dates its first contact; the end 18:00 is the start of evening (tolerances.json time.day_parts). corrected_claim.text: Blackford (July 17): "The corps was deployed 2 miles from Gettysburg, with the left resting upon the Heidlersburg pike", moved forward "driving in the cavalry vedettes", met "a large force of cavalry ... in line, with a heavy line of men dismounted as skirmishers": "The former charged us twice, but were easily repulsed. After an hour or more of active skirmishing, the enemy's infantry advanced in force through the town". Against the centre "no movement by any force heavier than a double line of sharpshooters, whom our men invariably drove back, charging them once in gallant style"; on the extreme left the enemy "advanced in three lines" and the men "retired, firing from tree to tree until they met Gordon's brigade advancing, after which they were rallied on the center at the sound of my bugle". Rodes: "the sharpshooters of the Alabama brigade, under that promising young officer, Major [Eugene] Blackford, of the Fifth Alabama"; O'Neal: "Major Blackford, commanding corps of sharpshooters". Union side: Devin's cavalry brigade was driven back "by the advance of the enemy's line of battle, coming from the direction of Heidlersburg" and held "the rebel line in check for two hours, until relieved by the arrival of the Eleventh Corps"; the 45th New York's skirmish line "encountered a battalion of Alabama sharpshooters, under Major Blackford, stretched along the lane at the foot of Oak Hill". No source names the Union cavalry that Blackford met (the identification with Devin's brigade is not made by either report) and none gives an hour for the skirmish, the repulse or the rally; the window opens at 12:00 with the first Confederate hours for the division and ends at the evening edge; the sharpshooters were ahead of the division, so the first contact may be earlier. No clock offset between Union and Confederate reports is applied.
corrected_claim.marking: skirmish, cavalry repulse, rally by bugle: documented; the hour: not stated in any report

sub_claims.claim: Blackford: the corps was deployed 2 miles from Gettysburg with its left on the Heidlersburg pike and moved steadily forward upon the town, driving in the cavalry vedettes posted in the road and on commanding hills
About half a mile from the suburbs a large force of cavalry was seen in line with a heavy line of men dismounted as skirmishers; the cavalry charged twice and was easily repulsed
After an hour or more of active skirmishing the enemy's infantry advanced in force through the town
Against the centre there was no movement by any force heavier than a double line of sharpshooters, whom the men invariably drove back, charging them once

On the extreme left the enemy advanced in three lines and drove in the men posted behind the trees; they retired firing from tree to tree until they met Gordon's brigade advancing and were then rallied on the centre at the sound of Blackford's bugle

The command is the corps (battalion) of sharpshooters of the Alabama brigade under Major Blackford of the Fifth Alabama Infantry (Rodes, O'Neal; the report is signed Comdg. Battalion of Sharpshooters)
Daniel (Rodes' division): his brigade was within about 2.5 miles of the town at about 12 m. when ordered to turn to the right

Hays (Early's division): Gordon's brigade was ordered to advance a little after 2 o'clock, the hour from which the rally of the sharpshooters on the extreme left, when they met Gordon's brigade advancing, can follow

Devin (Union cavalry): his skirmishers on the right were forced back by the advance of the enemy's line of battle coming from the direction of Heidlersburg and his brigade held the rebel line in check for two hours until relieved by the Eleventh Corps

45th New York sketch (1900): its skirmish line met a battalion of Alabama sharpshooters under Major Blackford stretched along the lane at the foot of Oak Hill to the apple orchard near Hagy's farm; the 61st Ohio and 74th Pennsylvania came into skirmish line on its right about 1 o'clock
The cavalry that Blackford met was Devin's brigade (same approach, before the Eleventh Corps deployed)
sub_claims.note: neither report names the other; the identification rests on place and time only

corrected_claim.event: Pender's division goes forward through and past Heth's division and attacks the First Corps line on Seminary Ridge: Hill orders it forward after about 2.30, keeping Thomas' brigade in reserve; Perrin is ordered forward again about 3 and, after 4 o'clock, ordered by Pender to advance and pass Heth's division; Scales advances under severe artillery fire, loses every field officer but one and is wounded; Lane covers the right flank against cavalry; Thomas remains in support until near sunset
corrected_claim.unit: Pender's division, Third Corps: Perrin's (McGowan's) brigade, Scales' brigade, Lane's brigade, Thomas' brigade; Wainwright's batteries and Gamble's dismounted cavalry opposing
corrected_claim.place: The ground west and north-west of the Lutheran seminary on both sides of the Cashtown pike (Seminary Ridge), the cavalry on the Union left south of it

time_window.text: Jul 1, about 14:30 (Hill's order) to about 17:00; the attack after 16:00 by Perrin's clock
time_window.basis: Hill OR27-2-R534 p.607; Perrin R557 pp.661-662; Scales R560 pp.669-670; Lane R558 p.665; Thomas R559 p.668; Wainwright OR27-1-R071 pp.356-357; Gamble R338 p.934; Doubleday R029 p.250; Pennsylvania at Gettysburg vol.1 p.493. Window limits: the start 14:30 is Hill's hour for the appearance of Ewell's right wing, after which Pender's division was ordered forward (about 2.30 o'clock, R534 p.607); the end 17:00 is Robinson's hour for the orders to withdraw reaching the Second Division, the last First Corps division to leave the line (nearly 5 p. m., R043 p.290). A limit is an allowed bound, not a claim of when the event happened; the reader adds its own clock tolerance at a clock-time limit.

corrected_claim.text: Hill: "About 2.30 o'clock, the right wing of Ewell's corps made its appearance on my left ... Pender's division was then ordered forward, Thomas' brigade being retained in reserve". Perrin: the brigade "remained in this position until about 3 o'clock, and were again ordered forward", then "probably until after 4 o'clock, when I was ordered by General Pender to advance, and to pass General Heth's division should I come up with it at a halt", and he "passed Brigadier-General Pettigrew's brigade, the men of which seemed much exhausted"; he found himself without support, Scales halted near the fence and Lane's brigade not in sight, and estimates the enemy artillery on the left "at least thirty pieces". Scales: advanced "after the lapse of some thirty minutes" under "severe artillery fire", "Every discharge made sad havoc", "Every field officer of the brigade save one had been disabled", he was wounded by a shell. Lane: deployed the Seventh North Carolina "to protect our flank, which was exposed to the enemy's cavalry", met cavalry and a few infantry from the woods and was ordered not to advance farther. Gamble: dismounted cavalry behind a stone wall opened "a sharp and rapid carbine fire" and fell back when overwhelmed. Thomas: moved to within about a mile in support of Heth's division and "remained until near sunset". Wainwright: twelve guns concentrated "hardly 5 yards apart" and Stewart's battery enfilading the line along the pike. The gun count: Wainwright has twelve guns concentrated beside Stewart's battery, Hunt (chief of artillery) sixteen guns concentrated (L 1st New York, 5th Maine, B 1st Pennsylvania) with Stewart's six 12-pounders on the same line (22 in all), Perrin an estimate of at least thirty pieces; the seed's "about 20 guns of Wainwright" devastating Scales lies among these and no report names Scales with a number of guns. NOT in any report or library text read: "a 50-yard gap between the 121st PA and Gamble's cavalry". The hours differ between orders and movements and are carried as scenarios; no clock offset is applied.
corrected_claim.marking: advance of Pender's division, Thomas in reserve, Lane and the cavalry: documented; gun count: sources differ (12-22); the link of about 20 guns to Scales and the 50-yard gap: not in any source read

sub_claims.claim: Hill: about 2.30 o'clock the right wing of Ewell's corps appeared on his left; Pender's division was then ordered forward, Thomas' brigade being retained in reserve
Hill: Perrin's brigade took position after position of the enemy and drove him through the town

Perrin: the brigade remained until about 3 o'clock and was again ordered forward; after 4 o'clock Pender ordered him to advance and pass Heth's division; he passed Pettigrew's brigade, the men much exhausted

Lane's brigade took position on Perrin's right to protect the flank from the enemy's cavalry (Perrin); later Perrin found Scales halted near the fence and Lane's brigade not moving on his right and not in sight

Scales: advanced after about thirty minutes' halt under severe artillery fire; every discharge made sad havoc; every field officer but one was disabled; he was wounded by a shell and the enemy gave way less than ten minutes after
Perrin: the whole of the enemy's artillery on the left, at least thirty pieces, was limbered up and moved to the rear

Wainwright: the enemy came up in two columns that outflanked the line by nearly a third of a mile, then in double line; twelve guns were concentrated hardly 5 yards apart and Stewart's battery enfiladed the line along the Cashtown pike

Lane: the Seventh North Carolina deployed to protect the right flank exposed to cavalry; cavalry and a few infantry opened from the woods; the enemy retreated to Cemetery Hill; Pender ordered Lane not to advance farther unless there was another general forward movement

Gamble: dismounted cavalry behind a stone wall opened a sharp and rapid carbine fire that killed and wounded many of the first line, and fell back when the enemy came very close, to the next ridge on the left of the town

Thomas: formed on the left of the road, advanced to within about 1 mile of Gettysburg in readiness to support Heth's division, and remained until near sunset, then took position near the town in support of artillery
A Pennsylvania address (1914 volume): Pender, about 3.30 o'clock, assailed the three small brigades of Stone, Morrow and Biddle

Number of guns on the Seminary Ridge line: Hunt has sixteen guns concentrated and Stewart's battery (six 12-pounders) on the same line, Wainwright twelve concentrated guns and Stewart's battery, Perrin an estimate of at least thirty pieces; the seed has about 20 guns of Wainwright
Scales' brigade was devastated by the fire of about 20 of Wainwright's guns (a link between Scales' report and a gun count)
sub_claims.note: Scales reports severe artillery fire and havoc in his ranks but names no guns; Wainwright and Hunt name no Confederate brigade for this fire

sub_claims.claim: Perrin breaks a 50-yard gap between the 121st Pennsylvania and Gamble's cavalry
sub_claims.note: no text read has the gap; A. Biddle (121st) says the line extended far beyond his left flank

corrected_claim.event: Doubleday orders the First Corps to fall back from the seminary line after the enemy, strongly re-enforced, advances in large numbers about 4 p. m.: Biddle's and Meredith's brigades cover the movement from the intrenchments (a barricade of rails) in front of the seminary that Doubleday had directed to be thrown up as a precaution; Wadsworth had already ordered his division to retire at 3.45; Howard's message about 4 p. m. and positive order at 4.10 follow
corrected_claim.unit: First Corps (Maj. Gen. Abner Doubleday): Biddle's brigade, Meredith's (Iron) brigade, Wadsworth's and Robinson's divisions, Cooper's and Stevens' batteries; Howard commanding the field
corrected_claim.place: Seminary Ridge: the line of rails and intrenchments in front of the Lutheran seminary, then through the town to Cemetery Hill

time_window.text: Jul 1, about 15:45 to 16:10 (Wadsworth 3.45; the enemy advance about 4; Howard 4.10); Doubleday gives no hour for his own order
time_window.basis: Doubleday OR27-1-R029 pp.250-251; Wadsworth R032 p.266; Howard R243 p.704; Rowley R055 p.313. Window limits: the start 15:45 is Wadsworth's hour for the order to retire (3.45 o'clock, quoted by Doubleday R029 p.251); the end 16:10 is Howard's positive order to the First and Eleventh Corps to fall back (4.10 p. m., R243 p.704). A limit is an allowed bound, not a claim of when the event happened; the reader adds its own clock tolerance at a clock-time limit.

corrected_claim.text: Doubleday: "About 4 p. m. the enemy, having been strongly re-enforced, advanced in large numbers ... It became necessary to retreat", then "I now gave orders to fall back, this and Meredith's brigades covering the movement by occupying the intrenchments in front of the seminary, which I had directed to be thrown up as a precautionary measure to assist in holding the new position"; "From behind the feeble barricade of rails these brave men ... held the rebel lines ... at bay until the greater portion of the corps had retired". Doubleday himself prints Wadsworth's report ("I ordered the command to retire at 3.45 o'clock") and says the written statements of the division commanders on the details of this period "are slightly conflicting". Howard: about 4 p. m. word to Doubleday to fall back, fighting; 4.10 positive order. The works in front of the seminary: Robinson says that on his arrival orders were received to hold the seminary and the First Brigade (Paul) was set at work to intrench the ridge; Farnham (16th Maine) that the regiment threw up a barricade of rails and was ordered to the right after fifteen minutes; the adjutant of the 16th Maine (Maine at Gettysburg, 1898) that by Robinson's command the First Brigade hastily threw up a redoubt of earth and fence rails just in front of the seminary and that about one o'clock the regiment was called out: the works were therefore built before about 13:00, by troops of Robinson's division on its arrival, with no hour in any report. NOT in any report: 16:30 (the seed's value from Wikipedia) as the hour of Doubleday's order, and an hour for building the works. Delegated decision C-043 applies the default 16:00 to the Union retreat order; the other hours stay selectable.
corrected_claim.marking: order after the 4 p. m. advance, intrenchments (rails) in front of the seminary: documented; 16:30 and the hour of building the rails: not in any report

sub_claims.claim: Doubleday: about 4 p. m. the enemy, strongly re-enforced, advanced in large numbers and it became necessary to retreat

Doubleday: he gave orders to fall back, Biddle's and Meredith's brigades covering the movement by occupying the intrenchments in front of the seminary which he had directed to be thrown up as a precaution
The remnant of the Iron Brigade and others held the rebel lines at bay from behind a feeble barricade of rails until the greater portion of the corps had retired
Rowley: the First Brigade fell back, firing, until it reached a cover of rails hastily thrown up by some of the other troops in front of the seminary

Robinson: on arriving he received orders to hold the seminary and Paul's First Brigade was set at work to intrench the ridge; Farnham (16th Maine): the regiment threw up a barricade of rails and after fifteen minutes was ordered to the right; the 16th Maine's adjutant (1898): by Robinson's command the First Brigade hastily threw up a redoubt of earth and fence rails just in front of the seminary, and about one o'clock the regiment was called out
Wadsworth (printed by Doubleday): he ordered the command to retire at 3.45 o'clock; Doubleday: the statements of the division commanders on the details of this period are slightly conflicting
Howard: about 4 p. m. word to Doubleday to fall back, fighting, to Cemetery Hill; at 4.10 p. m. a positive order to the First and Eleventh Corps to fall back gradually
Doubleday ordered the withdrawal at about 16:30 (Wikipedia)
sub_claims.note: no report gives 16:30

corrected_claim.text: Howard (10 p. m., Jul 1): "The loss in my corps is about 3,000 killed, wounded, and missing. In the two corps we have lost one piece of artillery". Howard (report): at 3.20 p. m. the enemy renewed his attack, Schurz, "engaged with a force of the enemy much larger than his own", asked for a brigade and Coster's brigade was pushed out "to cover the retreat"; at 4.10 "the troops were already giving way"; the movement was executed "with considerable confusion, on account of the First and Eleventh Corps coming together in the town"; at 4.30 "the columns reached Cemetery Hill"; "In passing through the town we lost many prisoners". Schurz: the retreat through the town was effected with the streets "filled with vehicles of every description and overrun with men of the First Corps"; "A considerable number of men ... were taken prisoners"; "It was after 5 o'clock when the Eleventh Corps occupied the position on Cemetery Hill"; "By the losses sustained in the battle of July 1, the Third Division was reduced to an effective force of about 1,500 men". Ewell: Early's and Rodes' divisions together "captured over 4,000 prisoners and three pieces of artillery"; Hill: "for the Third Corps, 2 pieces of artillery and 2,300 prisoners" (the Union corps are not distinguished). NOT in any report read: the seed's about 3,200 lost and about 1,400 prisoners for the Eleventh Corps (Wikipedia); the casualty return of the corps is a three-day figure (3,801 in a Pennsylvania volume) and the return table is unreadable in the OCR. The Jul 1 loss is therefore carried as a range from about 3,000 (Howard) to not more than the three-day total.
corrected_claim.marking: retreat, many prisoners, about 3,000 lost (Howard estimate): documented; about 3,200 and about 1,400 prisoners: not in any source read

corrected_claim.text: The repository ephemeris (two independent methods that agree within 0.01 degree over every minute of the table) gives altitude 37.870 and azimuth 269.945 degrees at 16:00 local mean time (LMT = UT + longitude / 15) on 1863-07-01. A third, independent low-precision computation (Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms, chapter 25; closeout/tools/sunpos.py) gives 37.876 and 269.942, so the seed values 37.9 and 270 are these rounded; the altitude is the geometric altitude of the sun's centre, without refraction. Sunset 19:32 and civil dusk 20:04 of the same table. The sky: no report or text read states a cloud cover for Jul 1 (row T1-132 found rain on the roads in the morning, sultry weather about noon and showers in the afternoon; the readings of Jacobs for Jul 1 are not in the 1864 text read); "overcast, so soft light" is therefore a weather-model value marked plausible-procedural, not a documented sky. The project clock is a convention (no standard time existed in 1863).

corrected_claim.event: Wainwright's batteries, not told of the retreat, are ordered to stay in position, then see the infantry rapidly retreating to the town, limber to the rear and move at a walk down the Cashtown pike until the infantry has left it, break into a trot when the pike is clear (too late to save everything: one gun and four caissons lost, 83 officers and men and about 80 horses lost in the day), and pass immediately through the town to Cemetery Hill
corrected_claim.unit: Wainwright's artillery brigade, First Corps: Stewart's (B, 4th US), Cooper's (B, 1st Pennsylvania), Stevens' (5th Maine), Reynolds' / Breck's (L, 1st New York) batteries; the seed counts 17 guns
corrected_claim.place: Seminary Ridge, the Cashtown pike under the railroad embankment, the open ground between the ridge and the town, the streets of the town, Cemetery Hill (the street is not named in the report)

time_window.text: Jul 1, about 15:45 to 16:30 (the retreat of the infantry after Wadsworth's 3.45; columns on Cemetery Hill 4.30)
time_window.basis: Wainwright OR27-1-R071 pp.356-357; Doubleday R029 p.251; Howard R243 p.704; Wadsworth R032 p.266. Window limits: the start 15:45 is Wadsworth's hour for the order to retire (3.45 o'clock, R032 p.266), the order Captain Stevens received to withdraw his battery (Wainwright R071 p.357); the end 16:30 is Howard's hour for the columns reaching Cemetery Hill (4.30 p. m., R243 p.704). A limit is an allowed bound, not a claim of when the event happened; the reader adds its own clock tolerance at a clock-time limit.

corrected_claim.text: Wainwright: Stevens received an order from Wadsworth to withdraw; "Not knowing that he had received such an order ... I directed all the batteries to remain in position. A few minutes, however, showed me our infantry rapidly retreating to the town. All the batteries were at once limbered to the rear, and moved at a walk down the Cashtown pike until the infantry had all left it and passed under cover of the railroad embankment"; enemy skirmishers then "opened a severe fire from behind a paling fence ... within 50 yards of the road"; "The pike being clear, the batteries now broke into a trot, but it was too late to save everything": Wilber's last piece was lost (horses shot), three caissons of Battery B, 4th US broke down and another was destroyed; the loss was "83 officers and men and about 80 horses"; "The batteries passed immediately through the town along with the other troops". Doubleday: the batteries lost heavily "as they retired to the town", the last gun left, "the horses being all shot down by the enemy's skirmishers, who had formed line within 50 yards of the road". NOT in any report or library text read: a gallop down Chambersburg Street three abreast and a count of 17 guns (the report has twelve guns concentrated beside Stewart's battery and gives no total).
corrected_claim.marking: walk down the Cashtown pike, trot, losses: documented; gallop down Chambersburg Street three abreast, 17 guns: not in any source read

Enemy skirmishers lapped the retreating columns and opened a severe fire from behind a paling fence within 50 yards of the road; the pike being clear, the batteries broke into a trot, too late to save everything
Losses: Wilber's last piece (horses shot), three caissons of Battery B, 4th US broke down; the battery losses of the day 83 officers and men and about 80 horses
The batteries passed immediately through the town along with the other troops and were placed on Cemetery Hill
Doubleday: the batteries lost heavily and the last gun was left, its horses shot down by skirmishers within 50 yards of the road
Howard: the columns reached Cemetery Hill at 4.30 p. m.
The batteries galloped down Chambersburg Street three abreast; 17 guns

corrected_claim.event: Captain Glenn's headquarters guard holds the seminary position for about twenty minutes while the last troops, ambulances and artillery retreat: Doubleday has Glenn defend the building for fully twenty minutes against a whole brigade; the 149th Pennsylvania's own account has Company D deploy near the Fairfield road, fire enough to make the enemy halt, help put one of Reynolds' guns in position and delay the rebels about twenty minutes
corrected_claim.unit: Capt. James Glenn commanding Doubleday's headquarters guard, Company D, 149th Pennsylvania Volunteers (Stone's brigade, Wadsworth's division, First Corps)
corrected_claim.place: The Lutheran seminary building on Seminary Ridge (Doubleday's headquarters); the 149th Pennsylvania places the company near the Fairfield road beside the seminary

time_window.text: Jul 1, about 15:45 to 16:30, after the line at the seminary was overpowered; no source gives an hour, only a duration of about twenty minutes
time_window.basis: Doubleday OR27-1-R029 p.251; the 149th Pennsylvania in Pennsylvania at Gettysburg vol.2 pp.746-747; Wadsworth R032 p.266; Howard R243 p.704. Window limits: the start 15:45 is Wadsworth's hour for the order to retire (3.45 o'clock, quoted by Doubleday R029 p.251); Glenn's stand came when "all the troops at this point were overpowered"; the end 16:30 is Howard's hour for the columns reaching Cemetery Hill (4.30 p. m., R243 p.704), which the artillery and the remaining troops reached after Glenn's stand. A limit is an allowed bound, not a claim of when the event happened; the reader adds its own clock tolerance at a clock-time limit.

corrected_claim.text: Doubleday: "When all the troops at this point were overpowered, Captain Glenn, of the One hundred and forty-ninth Pennsylvania Volunteers, in command of my headquarters guard, defended the building for fully twenty minutes against a whole brigade of the enemy, enabling the few remaining troops, the ambulances, artillery, &c., to retreat in comparative safety"; he himself "remained at the seminary superintending the final movement" until hostile bayonets appeared around the building. The regimental account of the 149th Pennsylvania (1914 volume): "Company D, of the One hundred and forty-ninth Regiment, under Captain Glenn, which had been acting as headquarter guard, was ordered to deploy near the Fairfield road, which they did, and opened a fire sufficient to induce the enemy to halt, supposing that our forces had made a stand there. At the same time they assisted some of the artillerymen to put one of Reynold's guns in position, from which three shots were fired. This action delayed the rebels about twenty minutes and enabled the artillerymen to take off all the guns except one, which was spiked and left." The two accounts agree on a stand of about twenty minutes and differ on place and manner (the building against a brigade; a line near the Fairfield road beside a gun). Neither gives an hour: the seed's 16:00-16:20 is not in either; the window is bounded by Wadsworth's 3.45 and Howard's 4.30. No clock offset is applied.
corrected_claim.marking: stand of about twenty minutes: documented (two sources); place and manner: two versions; hour: not stated

Where and how Glenn's company stood: defending the building against a whole brigade (Doubleday) or deployed near the Fairfield road beside a gun (149th Pennsylvania)
The regiment was engaged almost continuously from 11 a. m. until 4 p. m.; Wadsworth ordered the division to retire at 3.45; Howard has the columns on Cemetery Hill at 4.30: Glenn's stand lies between
The stand lasted from about 16:00 to 16:20 (seed)

corrected_claim.text: Farnham (OR): the regiment "ordered, alone, by General Robinson, to take possession of a hill which commanded the road, and hold the same as long as there was a man left", held until, "finding the enemy in such force" and no support, it fell back into the hollow and the woods and "ordered a retreat, but not in time to reach the main body of the brigade"; loss of the day 223 (officers killed 1, men killed 8, officers wounded 5, men wounded 47, officers missing 11, men missing 151). Maine at Gettysburg (1898): "It was about four o'clock in the afternoon when the Sixteenth Maine was ordered to advance", the order "Take the position and hold it at any cost"; "took position behind the stone wall, and broke the right wing to the right, parallel to the Mummasburg Road"; "In a short time, perhaps twenty minutes ... the enemy were upon them"; at the railroad cut Ewell's men and Hill's struck at once, "Colonel Tilden fell to Swell's share" (the OCR prints Swell for Ewell), "twelve officers and ninety-two enlisted men" were captured and "thirty-five in all, and four officers" escaped to Cemetery Hill; the marker: killed 11, wounded 62, captured 159 out of 275 engaged. corrected_claim.text: Early: Hays and Avery drove the second line "back into the town in great confusion", "Hays' brigade entered the town, fighting its way" and "was formed in line in the street running through the middle of the town"; "A very large number of prisoners were captured in the town, and before reaching it". Rodes: "My division followed him closely into and through the town, Doles and Ramseur entering in such close contact with the enemy" that Doles "had two sharp and successful encounters with the enemy in its streets". Hays: he "advanced through the city of Gettysburg, clearing it of the enemy and taking prisoners at every turn". Howard: "considerable confusion, on account of the First and Eleventh Corps coming together in the town" and "we lost many prisoners". Schurz: the streets "filled with vehicles of every description and overrun with men of the First Corps", men "entangled in cross streets and alleys, were taken prisoners", Schimmelfennig fell into the hands of rebel skirmishers "but succeeded in hiding himself until, on July 4". New York at Gettysburg (1900): "About 2,500 men, including 145 officers, were made prisoners during the retreat to the town and the passage through the place"; the 45th New York turned into an alley with no exit, "14 officers and 164 men were captured"; Schimmelfennig dodged into a woodshed on Baltimore Street under sticks of firewood "for three days"; Chaplain Howell "fell on the steps of the Lutheran Church on Chambersburg Street". NPS Handbook: Schimmelfennig "finding refuge in a shed, he lay 2 days concealed". NOT in any source read: Schimmelfennig in a "midden" (the seed's SS value) or a "woodpile" by that name; Union soldiers hiding in "fenced backyards". The shed, three days and two days differ and are carried.

corrected_claim.event: Hancock reaches Cemetery Hill and meets Howard: he gives 3 p. m. (report), Howard's 5 p. m. dispatch 4 p. m., his own 5.25 dispatch "an hour since" (about 4.25), Howard's narrative after 4.30; Howard says Hancock came, said Meade had sent him under the impression that he was Howard's senior, and "We agreed at once that that was no time for talking": Hancock to arrange the troops and place the batteries on the left of the Baltimore pike, Howard to take the right; Hancock reports to Meade "Howard says that Doubleday's command gave way"
corrected_claim.unit: Maj. Gen. W. S. Hancock (Second Corps) and Maj. Gen. O. O. Howard (Eleventh Corps), with Brig. Gen. G. K. Warren and Brig. Gen. J. Buford assisting
corrected_claim.place: Cemetery Hill, south of Gettysburg (the line on and near the Baltimore pike)

time_window.text: Jul 1, 15:00 to about 16:30 (four primary values; the delegated default is about 15:00-16:00)
time_window.basis: Hancock OR27-1-R076 pp.366, 368; Howard R243 pp.696, 704; Slocum R271 p.768; Pierce, Battle of Gettysburg (1914). Window limits: the start 15:00 is Hancock's own hour of arrival (3 p. m., R076 p.368); the end 16:30 is Howard's hour at which the columns reached Cemetery Hill (4.30 p. m., R243 p.704), after which Hancock "came to me about this time". A limit is an allowed bound, not a claim of when the event happened; the reader adds its own clock tolerance at a clock-time limit.

corrected_claim.text: Howard (report): "General Hancock came to me about this time, and said General Meade had sent him on hearing the state of affairs; that he had given him his instructions while under the impression that he was my senior. We agreed at once that that was no time for talking, and that General Hancock should further arrange the troops, and place the batteries upon the left of the Baltimore pike, while I should take the right of the same." Hancock (report): the position "was already partially occupied on my arrival by direction of Major-General Howard" and "In forming the lines, I received material assistance from Major-General Howard, Brigadier-Generals Warren and Buford"; his 5.25 p. m. dispatch to Meade: "When I arrived here an hour since ... Howard says that Doubleday's command gave way". Howard's evening letter: "I believe I have handled these two corps to-day from a little past 11 until 4, when General H. assisted me in carrying out orders which I had already issued". Hancock says 3 p. m. (report), Howard and Slocum 4 p. m., Hancock's dispatch about 4.25 and Howard's narrative after 4.30; a 1914 address gives 3.30 (OCR). The seed values (before 16:00, Civil War Monitor) have no non-lead source; no clock offset is applied.
corrected_claim.marking: arrival hours as scenarios, delegated default about 15:00-16:00; the exchange: documented (Howard's account; Hancock's does not describe it)

sub_claims.claim: Hancock's report: at 3 p. m. he arrived at Gettysburg and assumed command; the First and Eleventh Corps were retiring through the town
Howard's 5 p. m. dispatch: General Hancock arrived at 4 p. m. and communicated his instructions; Slocum: Howard commanded until 4 p. m., when relieved by Hancock
Hancock's 5.25 p. m. dispatch to Meade: "When I arrived here an hour since"; "Howard says that Doubleday's command gave way"

Howard's narrative: at 4.30 the columns reached Cemetery Hill; Hancock came to him about this time, said Meade had sent him and had given his instructions under the impression that he was Howard's senior; they agreed at once that it was no time for talking, Hancock to arrange the troops and place the batteries on the left of the Baltimore pike, Howard to take the right
Hancock: the position on Cemetery Hill was already partially occupied on his arrival by direction of Howard; he received material assistance from Howard, Warren and Buford in forming the lines
Howard's evening letter: he had handled the two corps from a little past 11 until 4, when Hancock assisted him in carrying out orders already issued
Pierce (1914): at 3.30 p. m. Hancock comes riding up with orders from Meade to take command, although junior in rank to Howard (OCR "3 130 p. M" read as 3.30)

corrected_claim.text: Hancock: "Orders were at once given to establish a line of battle on Cemetery Hill, with skirmishers occupying that part of the town immediately in our front"; Wadsworth's division and a battery (thought to be the Fifth Maine) "were placed on the eminence just across the turnpike"; Geary's division went "to the high ground to the right of and near Round Top Mountain"; he sent Meade a communication "informing him that the position at Gettysburg was a very strong one, having for its disadvantage that it might be easily turned, and leaving to him the responsibility whether the battle should be fought at Gettysburg or at a place first selected by him". His 5.25 dispatch: "We have now taken up a position in the cemetery, and cannot well be taken. It is a position, however, easily turned ... I think we can retire; if not, we can fight here". Howard: after learning of Reynolds' death (about 11.30) he "came to the conclusion that the only tenable position for my limited force was the ridge to the southeast of Gettysburg, now so well known as Cemetery Ridge" and set up headquarters near the cemetery; Wadsworth's division "was sent to occupy a height to the right and rear of our position". Meade: "the reports from Major-Generals Hancock and Howard on the character of the position being favorable, I determined to give battle at this point". Howard's evening letter: "This evening I have read an order stating that if General Slocum was present he would assume command ... The above has mortified me and will disgrace me." NOT in any text read: Doubleday's statement that Howard resisted and Hancock's marginal note denying it (neither book is in the library; Howard's own account is that they "agreed at once"); Hancock choosing Gettysburg as the battlefield (the reports have Howard choosing the ground and Meade deciding the battle).
corrected_claim.marking: dispositions, Wadsworth to the eminence, Geary to Round Top, Howard's choice of the ridge: documented; Hancock selecting Gettysburg: contradicted; Doubleday's and Hancock's notes: not found

corrected_claim.text: Brabble (32nd NC): "about 2.30 p. m., the regiment was drawn up on the right of the brigade, and, advancing, met the enemy about 4 o'clock"; near the railroad cut and a large stone barn "the enemy was strongly posted"; the brigade could not cross the cut at first, the regiment charged to the barn, was driven back, then after the brigade changed direction it moved up beyond the barn and "advanced near the edge of town"; "it took a considerable number of prisoners". Lewis (43rd NC): "At the railroad cut, 400 or 500 prisoners surrendered to the brigade; also several stand of colors". Hopkins (45th NC): "capturing 188 prisoners in this place [the wood] and several smaller squads". Daniel: "About this time a body of troops ... belonged to Major-General Pender's division, commenced a most spirited advance on my right", "I succeeded in taking the hill, with a very heavy loss. Here a very large number of prisoners were captured" and the command "continued to move forward until it reached the outskirts of the town"; the loss "about one-third the number that entered the fight". NOT in any report: 16:30 (the seed's Wikipedia value) as the hour of the renewed assault; the surrender of "about 500" is Lewis's "400 or 500" at the cut. The 2nd NC Battalion and the 43rd NC date their entry into the engagement from about 12 m. to 1 p. m.; no clock offset is applied.

corrected_claim.text: Steinwehr: he arrived about 2 o'clock, "placed the First Brigade, Col. Charles R. Coster, on the northeast end of the hill, in support of Wiedrich's battery", then "ordered Colonel Coster to advance with his brigade through the town, to report to General Schurz", who "ordered him to take a position north and east of Gettysburg, and to check the advance of the enemy"; "Colonel Coster had a severe engagement with the advancing enemy, but was, of course, not strong enough to restore the battle", fell back to Cemetery Hill "leaving one regiment to occupy the nearest brick houses of the town". Schurz: Coster's brigade appeared, he deployed it "on the right of the junction of the roads near the railroad depot" and it checked the enemy long enough "to permit the First Division to enter the town". Howard: Steinwehr was permitted to push out Coster's brigade beyond the town "to cover the retreat". Bachelder: Hoke's brigade "was met near the brickyard, in the suburbs of the town, by Coster's brigade ... The engagement was of short duration. Coster was soon forced to retire to Cemetery Hill". Hunt: Heckman's battery "held his ground until the enemy entered his battery. He then retired with the loss of one gun", and the guns lost in the retiring of the two corps were two (Wilber's piece and Heckman's one). Battles and Leaders: Coster's brigade loss "w, 228 ; m. 314 = 597" for the battle. NOT in any source read: "313 captured" (the order of battle gives 314 missing for the three days), the loss of two of four guns by Coster's brigade (it had no guns of its own; Hunt has one gun of Heckman's four lost), and an hour for the engagement.
corrected_claim.marking: engagement, retreat to Cemetery Hill: documented (no hour); 313 captured, 2 of 4 guns: not in any source read (314 missing in three days; one gun of Heckman's)

corrected_claim.text: Ewell: "Early entering by the York Railroad at the same time that Rodes came in on the Cashtown road, they together captured over 4,000 prisoners and three pieces of artillery"; "no other troops than those of this corps entered the town at all". Rodes: his first line extended "from the left of the center of the town along one of its principal streets and out on the road to Fairfield"; the second line (Daniel and O'Neal) along the railroad. Early: "Hays' brigade was formed in line in the street running through the middle of the town". Hill: "These two divisions were bivouacked in the positions won". Perrin: the charge went on "until we got within 200 yards of their last position, about the theological college". Doubleday: he "remained at the seminary superintending the final movement" until "thousands of hostile bayonets made their appearance around the sides of the building". Jacobs (1864): "At the close of the fight, Ewell's corps occupied the town"; Rodes' division "occupying Middle street as far west as the Seminary hill"; "Hill's corps took position on the Seminary ridge"; "General Lee had reconnoitred our position from the College cupola". Bachelder (1873): "The Seminary building was directly in the line of the Confederate army after the first day's fight; and was occupied as a hospital during and after the battle" (1889: "occupied during and after the battle as a Union hospital"); the College "used as a Confederate hospital". Hospital Scenes (1864): "sharp-shooters, who were on the tops of the houses"; Tillie Pierce: sharpshooters "would enter the cellar in search of eatables"; NPS: Federal soldiers "cut off from friendly lines, hid in cellars and outbuildings". The sources for the houses, the food and the cellars describe the days of the battle, not the afternoon of Jul 1 alone; no source gives an hour for the taking of the seminary building or of Pennsylvania Hall, which the 45th New York was preparing to defend about 4 p. m.; no clock offset is applied.
corrected_claim.marking: entry into the town, Seminary Ridge, the hospitals: documented; hour of the seminary and Pennsylvania Hall: not stated; houses and food: days of the battle

Window limits: the start 12:00 is Hard: "it was not until after noon that the Eleventh corps came to our relief"; the hospital then came under fire and the wounded were moved to the church; the end 17:30 is the end of the retreat of the Eleventh Corps through the town (row T1-162: columns on Cemetery Hill 4.30, corps in position after 5): the surgeons left the church while that retreat filled the street. A limit is an allowed bound, not a claim of when the event happened; the reader adds its own clock tolerance at a clock-time limit.

corrected_claim.text: Hard (surgeon of the 8th Illinois Cavalry, writing in 1868): it was not until after noon that the Eleventh Corps came to the cavalry's relief; the enemy's batteries then opened and the hospital at the depot came into their range; "We removed our wounded to the Presbyterian church near the center of the town, and were engaged in amputating the arm of a rebel soldier, when a messenger announced a dispatch from General Buford that we must fall back"; surgeons Beck, Rulison and Vosburg were left to attend the wounded and the others left the church "to find the street crowded by the retreating Eleventh corps". The Gettysburg National Park Commission's list of hospital tablets of the Army of the Potomac reads "The Cavalry Corps in front of the Presbyterian Church Gettysburg", and the National Park Service treatment plan names "the Cavalry Brigade Hospital Tablet" on the front of the church. Letterman says only that four ambulances of the Cavalry Corps were ordered left at Gettysburg. NOT documented: that it was a Cavalry Corps hospital as a whole (the text is the 8th Illinois Cavalry's own hospital; the tablet is the Commission's), a capture of the church as an event with an hour, the hour of the move or of the departure, and the seed's evening (the surgeons left while the Eleventh Corps was retreating, afternoon). The Official Records do not mention the church; the HMDB marker 17939 cited by the seed could not be read (the host did not serve the page).

corrected_claim.text: The Historic Structures Report: "McPherson lost no buildings" (against Herbst's barn, burned); the tenant family "stayed on until the house burned down in the spring of 1895"; Lieutenant R. B. Beath of the 88th Pennsylvania passed himself off as a surgeon's assistant on July 1 and "upon reaching McPherson's barn he found it full of bleeding and mangled soldiers"; a chaplain entering later: "the barn was crowded with the wounded of both armies"; the report's own judgement: "The Confederate hospitals, granted, were further south than McPherson's farm buildings", the Southerners "should have made an effort to set up a field hospital there ... in ignoring those Yankees within the stone barn, they also overlooked the pained men from Virginia and North Carolina"; men "of the 55th Virginia" fired at the Union colour guard at the barnyard lane. Wainwright: "At dusk, no attack having been made, the batteries on the hill outside the cemetery gate were posted as follows, and light earthworks thrown up in front of each gun"; Coulter: the brigade, having moved to the left of the Eleventh Corps, "having built breastworks of such materials as were at hand" remained in support of the batteries.
